course.title: QuickBite — Software Engineering Laboratory
course.summary: One continuous team project across 20 meetings. This website is the authoritative QuickBite brief, task guide and submission checklist. General lecture examples illustrate other companies; they do not supply hidden QuickBite facts.

scenario.problem: QuickBite is a proposed food-ordering and delivery service. The company wants one digital flow for placing, fulfilling and tracking orders, but the brief intentionally leaves important engineering decisions open.
brief_points: Local restaurants currently use different ways to receive and confirm orders, which makes the customer experience inconsistent.
Customers need clearer information about whether an order was accepted, prepared, handed to delivery and completed.
Restaurants need a workable way to accept or reject incoming orders and communicate fulfilment status.
Delivery work must be coordinated with restaurant readiness without building a real route-optimization or GPS platform.
Payment and notification capabilities may be provided by external services; QuickBite should coordinate with them rather than implement real payment processing.
The teaching project uses synthetic data. Your team must decide and justify many details instead of trying to guess one hidden solution.
company_profile: QuickBite is a fictional company planning a food-ordering and delivery service. It is a proposal to analyse and design, not an existing production platform you must build.

The company wants a coherent information flow between customers, participating restaurants and couriers. Existing restaurant practices differ; confirmation and fulfilment status are unclear to customers.

The intended improvement is fewer coordination problems and clearer order status. The company has not supplied measured baselines, demand forecasts, budgets or financial results. Targets and numbers selected for the laboratory are teaching assumptions.

The course project is an engineering evidence portfolio: decisions, requirements, models, experiments and a small Python policy laboratory. The workbench website is the tool for this portfolio; it is not the production QuickBite application.
process_context: A customer browses a participating restaurant menu and prepares an order. The proposal includes order placement and a synthetic payment status.
The restaurant may accept or reject the order. Accepted orders are prepared and made ready; delivery is coordinated with a courier.
The customer needs meaningful status information through this flow. Notifications, cancellation and basic administration are part of the analysis.

This narrative does not settle timing, cancellation windows, assignment algorithms, retries, access rules or error recovery. Define these decisions consistently in your requirements, models and tests; label assumptions.
open_decisions: What may be cancelled, by whom, and until which stage?
When are payment confirmation, restaurant acceptance and courier assignment coordinated?
How should rejected orders, pending/declined payment, unavailable couriers and failed notifications be handled?
Which information may each role access and modify?
Which quality targets, business measures and operational assumptions are reasonable for this teaching proposal?
How would you separate responsibilities, choose a lifecycle and respond to a change?
data_rules: Use synthetic data only: invented restaurants, menu items, prices, order IDs and payment statuses. Do not collect real customer identities or card data.
No real company budget, demand, availability measurement or service-level agreement has been supplied. Do not report default simulator numbers as measured company facts.

The M10 policy lab is an explicit exception: published function contracts are fixed exercise rules. Compare them with your earlier design, document differences and test the published contracts without rewriting them to match your own assumptions.

modules.title: Project vision, software process and feasibility
theory: A fact is explicitly supplied by the brief; an assumption is your unverified working proposition; a constraint limits choices; an open question needs clarification. Keep these four lists separate. A stakeholder is anyone affected by the proposed change, including external organizations, not only a user role. For each, record need, concern and a question. A conflict is a tension between needs that cannot both be maximized.

Problem: [who] experiences [difficulty], causing [impact]. Vision: describe the desired improvement, not the technology. Scope defines capabilities and exclusions. A business objective has an outcome, metric, target/direction and way to measure it; a feature is not an outcome. Example for an unrelated service: reduce repeated booking corrections, measured per month. Invented baselines/targets must be marked as assumptions. Respect classroom constraints; decide your own project scope.

Sequential development plans major stages in order and suits relatively stable agreed needs. Iterative work revisits decisions with feedback; incremental work delivers useful slices progressively. Risk-driven work tackles the most consequential uncertainties first. Compare at least two approaches against requirement uncertainty, feedback access and risk/coordination; a hybrid needs a reason. These are ways to organize the hypothetical project, not instructions to deploy a live business.

Technical: can the proposed capabilities be achieved with plausible skills/technology? Operational: can people use and support the process? Economic: do assumed benefits justify assumed costs? Schedule: is the proposed effort/time plausible? Feasibility simulator uses synthetic PLN: build_cost is one-time development cost, monthly_benefit the estimated monetary benefit, monthly_cost recurring cost, months the analysis horizon. Monthly net = benefit − cost; net_value = months × monthly net − build_cost; payback = build_cost / monthly net if positive, otherwise no payback. This is undiscounted arithmetic, excluding tax, inflation and financing, not a real investment appraisal.

A base case is your starting set of assumptions. A sensitivity run asks “what if an assumption changes?” Keep the base inputs for comparison. For example, test build_cost × 1.2 to ask about a cost overrun, then monthly_benefit × 0.8 to ask about weaker benefits; 20% is an illustrative choice, not a company fact. Choose your own questions and changes. Save each of the three runs with Assign evidence to M01, then reference its saved filename and interpret net_value/payback in the report. You may use the default base values as explicitly labelled teaching assumptions; real prices are not required.

A risk is an uncertain future event, unlike an issue that has already happened. Record ID, cause/event, consequence and response/mitigation. Consider technical, operational, economic and schedule uncertainty separately. GO needs a defensible basis; CONDITIONAL GO names conditions that must be resolved; NO-GO explains unacceptable barriers. Five risks are a classroom minimum, not proof of completeness.

modules.title: Requirements engineering and traceability
theory: Elicit needs, analyse ambiguity/conflict, specify obligations, validate them and manage changes. Business requirements express outcomes; functional requirements specify services/behaviour; non-functional requirements constrain quality or operation. Use one main obligation per requirement and split compound statements. Choose your own coverage of your saved QuickBite scope rather than copy a ready-made solution.

Use a table with ID, type, requirement, source, priority, rationale and acceptance criterion. IDs remain stable when wording changes. Sources may be brief facts, M01 decisions or explicitly labelled assumptions. State a simple priority scale, such as must/should/could, and use it consistently. Acceptance criteria describe observable evidence; avoid “fast”, “easy” or “secure” without measurable conditions.

For an NFR specify metric, measurement condition/window and target; justify its stakeholder/risk relevance and label invented targets. A user story may use “As [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]”. An acceptance scenario may use Given [context], When [event], Then [observable result]. Include success, failure and boundary cases: for an unrelated booking service a boundary could be exactly the last permitted cancellation time.

Create goal ID → requirement ID → planned model/test evidence. Mark future evidence “planned”; do not pretend it exists. An orphan has no justified upstream goal/source or expected evidence. Review for ambiguity, multiple obligations, contradictions, omissions and unverifiable wording. Preserve before/after wording and why it changed; peer review may confirm a requirement as well as find a fault.

theory_cards.title: Quality and user-oriented scenarios

theory_cards.title: Traceability and review
theory_cards.body: Create goal ID → requirement ID → planned model/test evidence. Mark future evidence “planned”; do not pretend it exists. modules.title: Structured analysis and information flow
theory: A context model shows the entire system as one process plus external entities and named information flows. A level-1 DFD decomposes that transformation into processes and data stores. Process names describe transformations; flow/store names describe information, not clicks. Data must be transformed by a process: avoid entity→store or store→store links without a process.

All information crossing the context boundary must be accounted for at level 1. Internal stores/flows may be added, but do not silently add or remove external inputs/outputs. A balancing table records each context flow, matching level-1 flows and whether it is preserved, split/aggregated or unmatched. Explain renaming and aggregation. DFD models information transformation; M03 activity models order, decisions and control.

For each core structure define name, purpose, key fields/elements and useful type/constraints; use the same names across requirements and flows. For permissions make a role × resource table with read/create/update/delete or other meaningful actions. Mark explicit denied actions and justify them from responsibilities or risk. Do not infer blanket access from a role name.

Describe an asset/information item, plausible event, cause and consequence, then a control and a verification idea. For example in an unrelated booking system, one branch seeing another branch’s private notes could be prevented by scoped access and checked with a forbidden-access test. This is analysis using synthetic examples, not a request to attack a real system.

modules.title: Reliability, availability, fault tolerance and security
theory: Reliability concerns continuity of correct service; availability concerns readiness for use. A reachable service returning incorrect totals can be available but unreliable. Describe failure and stakeholder impact, then measurable requirements with conditions and time windows. Targets here are teaching assumptions, not real measured service levels.

mtbf_hours is assumed mean time between failures; mttr_hours is assumed mean repair time. Single-app availability A = MTBF/(MTBF+MTTR). With n independent replicas and perfect failover, app availability = 1−(1−A)^n. Required database availability multiplies this result (series dependency). modules.title: Class modeling and design patterns
theory: Find concepts and responsibilities in requirements/use cases/data definitions, merge duplicates, and separate domain concepts from UI widgets or technical plumbing. A class shows name, attributes and operations; relationships describe collaboration/structure. Multiplicity is the allowed number at an association end: 1, 0..1, 0..* or 1..*. In the simplified editor include multiplicities and relationship meaning in labels, with explanations in the report.

Patterns respond to recurring design pressures. Factory-like construction selects a creation variant; Adapter translates an external interface into your own interface; Strategy separates interchangeable behaviour behind one responsibility. These illustrate creational, structural and behavioural approaches. Compare at least two approaches, including no formal pattern if useful; choose one justified approach and explain consequences. Only one pattern decision is required, not three sketches or production implementations.

Packages group related responsibilities. Cohesion concerns how strongly a group belongs together; coupling concerns dependence between groups. Show major dependency arrows and inspect unnecessary cycles/ripple effects. Walk a proposed rule change through classes, operations and packages, noting boundaries that contain it. Explain at least two non-obvious design choices and alternatives.

modules.title: Software testing, Python defect repair and release
theory: Unit tests check a small function; integration tests check collaboration; system tests check the whole system; acceptance tests check stakeholder criteria. These are levels, not case-selection techniques. Prioritize rules/risks and explain untested areas. The executed lab covers policies.py, not a fully implemented food-delivery platform. Expected results must come from published contracts, not copying current buggy outputs.

For each case record ID, requirement/contract, initial condition/input, expected result and rationale. Include typical valid values, values just below/at/above a boundary, invalid input and legal/illegal state transitions. Treat bool, NaN and infinity according to the contract where applicable. Distinguish planned project-level cases from executable policy tests.

In Python testing select workspace/tests/test_student.py. Import unittest and policies as the starter shows. Test methods begin test_. self.assertEqual(actual, expected) checks a result; with self.assertRaises(ValueError): followed by an indented call checks a rejected input. For an unrelated helper double(3), expected 6 must come from its stated rule. Save code, then Run my tests only. Add at least six original tests across three contract behaviours before revealing the supplied suite; the starter placeholder alone does not meet the requirement.

FAIL means an assertion did not match; ERROR means execution raised unexpectedly. Read test name, traceback and expected/actual values, reproduce and isolate the contract mismatch, change implementation, then rerun. There are three intentional policy defects. Do not change public names/contracts or supplied tests. Record symptom, cause, fix and verification for each; the site keeps separate timestamped logs so failing and passing evidence survive.

Run all tests after repair. Passing totals only cover executed cases, not the entire hypothetical system. Record residual assumptions/risks and a RELEASE/CONDITIONAL RELEASE/DO NOT RELEASE classroom decision. Export your project ZIP including reports, models, saved runs, policy code, original tests, log history and a read-only assignment guide. It is imported on this website, not a standalone runnable server; production deployment is out of scope.

Run the complete suite, update defect notes and summarize residual limitations.

theory_cards.title: Test strategy and independent oracle
theory_cards.body: Unit tests check a small function; integration tests check collaboration; system tests check the whole system; acceptance tests check stakeholder criteria. These are levels, not case-selection techniques. Prioritize rules/risks and explain untested areas. The executed lab covers policies.py, not a fully implemented food-delivery platform. Expected results must come from published contracts, not copying current buggy outputs.

theory_cards.title: Selecting cases
theory_cards.body: For each case record ID, requirement/contract, initial condition/input, expected result and rationale. Include typical valid values, values just below/at/above a boundary, invalid input and legal/illegal state transitions. Treat bool, NaN and infinity according to the contract where applicable. Distinguish planned project-level cases from executable policy tests.

theory_cards.title: Python/unittest quick start
theory_cards.body: In Python testing select workspace/tests/test_student.py. Import unittest and policies as the starter shows. Test methods begin test_. self.assertEqual(actual, expected) checks a result; with self.assertRaises(ValueError): followed by an indented call checks a rejected input. For an unrelated helper double(3), expected 6 must come from its stated rule. Save code, then Run my tests only. Add at least six original tests across three contract behaviours before revealing the supplied suite; the starter placeholder alone does not meet the requirement.

theory_cards.title: Reading failures and repairing
theory_cards.body: FAIL means an assertion did not match; ERROR means execution raised unexpectedly. Read test name, traceback and expected/actual values, reproduce and isolate the contract mismatch, change implementation, then rerun. There are three intentional policy defects. Do not change public names/contracts or supplied tests. Record symptom, cause, fix and verification for each; the site keeps separate timestamped logs so failing and passing evidence survive.

theory_cards.title: Release evidence and limits
theory_cards.body: Run all tests after repair. Passing totals only cover executed cases, not the entire hypothetical system. Record residual assumptions/risks and a RELEASE/CONDITIONAL RELEASE/DO NOT RELEASE classroom decision. Export your project ZIP including reports, models, saved runs, policy code, original tests, log history and a read-only assignment guide. It is imported on this website, not a standalone runnable server; production deployment is out of scope.
